teachingContexts.title: Classifying Data

methods.statement: Distinguish a variable—the characteristic described, measured or counted—from its recorded data values.
Classify quantities, counts and measurements as numerical; classify descriptions, names and category labels as categorical, including numerical codes used as labels.
Classify numerical data as discrete when values are distinct and separate, usually from counting, or continuous when any value in a range is possible, usually from measuring.
Classify categorical data as nominal when categories have no natural order or ordinal when categories have a natural order; use the meaning of the categories to justify the classification.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching establishes variables and recorded values, then a two-level classification hierarchy: numerical data are discrete or continuous, and categorical data are nominal or ordinal. Guided responses consistently justify classifications using counting, measurement and natural ordering. All supplied theory, examples, matching responses and Key Ideas were inspected; no consequential contradictions were found. This context supports variable definition and data-type classification, with subtype classification the most advanced taught skill.

teachingContexts.title: Misleading Graphs

methods.statement: Distinguish correct underlying data from a graphical presentation that creates a false impression.

Check vertical-axis baselines, scale regularity and missing scales. Explain how a nonzero baseline can distort comparisons of bar lengths, while a clearly labelled restricted scale can appropriately reveal variation in a line graph.
Check whether data has been cherry picked or an inappropriate graph type has been used, and explain the resulting misleading impression.
Recognise that misleading presentations may arise accidentally or deliberately; the listed misleading features are not exhaustive.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The supplied teaching develops critique of misleading graphs through axis scales, selective data and unsuitable representations. Its baseline clarification appropriately distinguishes bar-length distortion from useful restricted scales in line graphs. The central assessed skill is explaining misleading graphs. No models or guided responses were supplied.

teachingContexts.title: Column Graphs

methods.statement: Represent quantities or frequencies across categories with a column graph, using a relevant title, category labels and a vertical-axis label with units where needed.
Start the numerical scale at zero, use consistent intervals, and draw equal-width columns with equal gaps. Include a matching key for paired series.
Construct the guided colour-frequency graph with one unit per grid row and column heights red 5, green 2, orange 7 and blue 3.
Read each graph using its own scale and interpret quantities in context: the tallest column represents the greatest quantity, while a shorter race time represents faster performance.
Calculate a percentage as the relevant count divided by the total count, multiplied by 100%, and use the approximation symbol for rounded results.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching covers column-graph construction conventions, contextual interpretation and percentages from counts. The guided response correctly converts the four table frequencies into separated, equal-width columns on a uniform scale starting at zero, with a title and both axis labels. The supplied short answer, worked method and editable solution diagram agree with the data and theory.

teachingContexts.title: Line Graphs

methods.statement: Use line graphs for readings in a meaningful order, usually time, including counts over time. Do not join unrelated categories because intermediate positions have no meaning.

Label axes, include relevant units and use consistent scales. Plot each data pair and join consecutive readings with straight segments. The guided model places time horizontally and water temperature vertically.

Estimate values between measurements by reading from the connecting segment to the relevant axis. At 10:15, halfway between the 24°C and 30°C readings, the estimated temperature is 27°C; averaging the endpoint temperatures checks this midpoint estimate.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching covers appropriate ordered data, consistent graph scales and axis labels, construction by plotting and joining consecutive readings, and interpolation from straight connecting segments. The guided table, completed graph and responses agree: temperatures are 20, 24, 30, 26 and 22°C at ten-minute intervals, with an estimated 27°C at 10:15. No consequential contradictions were identified.

teachingContexts.title: Dot Plots

methods.statement: Construct a dot plot above an evenly spaced numerical axis, placing one dot per observation and stacking repeated values vertically at equal intervals. Label the scale with the variable and units. The guided temperature plot correctly represents 12 observations with frequencies 17:1, 18:2, 19:2, 20:4, 21:2 and 22:1.
Read an explicit key before interpreting frequencies; a stated key may make each dot represent several observations instead of one.

Use stack heights to read frequencies and the distribution of numerical positions to identify clusters, gaps and possible outliers. The guided responses correctly identify concentration around 18–21°C and no clear outliers because no value is conspicuously separated.
Recognise numerical data as the data plotted on the taught number-line dot plot. Distinguish numerical distances, gaps and clusters from spacing between categories in a category-count display.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching develops dot-plot construction and interpretation using numerical data, equal scale spacing, vertical frequency stacks and explicit keys. The guided temperature example combines construction with identifying clusters and possible outliers; its data, completed plot and responses agree. Reflections reinforce numerical positioning and the display's usefulness for showing frequency and distribution, while distinguishing categorical spacing from numerical gaps.

teachingContexts.title: Stem-and-Leaf Plots

methods.statement: Separate numerical values into stems containing all digits except the last and leaves containing the final digit; use an explicit key to establish place values and units.

Construct an ordered plot with one leaf per observation, retaining repeated values and zero leaves and including empty stems within the data range. Check that the total number of leaves matches the number of observations.
Read back-to-back plots using the shared stem and the appropriate side's key. Order left-side observations from smallest to largest moving outwards from the stem.

For negative values, apply the minus sign to the complete stem-and-leaf value, including values shown with stem −0. Decreasing leaf digits represent increasing negative values moving outwards from the stem.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching establishes place-value construction and reading of stem-and-leaf plots, with explicit keys, ordered observations, repetitions, zero leaves and empty intermediate stems. The sit-up model correctly represents all ten observations. Guided reading extends the method to both sides of a back-to-back plot and to negative temperatures, including stem −0; the supplied responses agree with the displayed plots.

teachingContexts.title: Sector and Divided-Bar Graphs

methods.statement: Interpret sector and divided-bar graphs as parts of one whole: percentages total 100% and sector angles total 360°.
Find a category frequency by multiplying the whole by its share; recover the whole by dividing a known frequency by its share. Compare amounts with attention to the size of each whole.
Construct sector angles using frequency divided by total, multiplied by 360°; construct divided-bar segment lengths using the same share multiplied by the bar length.
Recognise a semicircle as one-half or 50%, and a right-angle sector as one-quarter or 25%.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching connects proportional graph interpretation with construction of sector and divided-bar graphs. The guided spending graph consistently shows Food as 30% and Rent as 40%; dividing $90 by 0.30 gives total spending of $300, then multiplying $300 by 0.40 gives rent of $120. All supplied theory, diagram and guided responses are consistent.

teachingContexts.title: Frequency Distribution Tables

methods.statement: Count occurrences of each value or category to construct a frequency distribution table, including zero for listed values that were not observed.
Find the number of observations by adding all frequencies, denoted by Σf. The household examples total 10 households.
Find a total numerical quantity by multiplying each value by its frequency and adding the products. The computers example gives 14 computers.
Identify the highest observed value as the largest value with a nonzero frequency. The highest observed number is 3 computers.
Identify the most frequent value by locating the greatest frequency. In the computers example, 2 computers occurs in 4 households.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The supplied teaching develops frequency-table construction and interpretation: counting occurrences, summing frequencies to count observations, calculating total quantities using value–frequency products, and identifying the highest observed and most frequent values. It explicitly distinguishes a listed value with zero frequency from an observed value. All supplied theory and guided responses are consistent; household counts and total computers retain their distinct meanings and units.

teachingContexts.title: Frequency Histograms and Polygons

methods.statement: Place numerical values on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis, using labelled axes and consistent scales.
Place histogram boundaries halfway between adjacent values and draw touching, equal-width columns with heights equal to frequencies. Preserve the interval for a zero frequency.
Construct a frequency polygon by joining column-top centres. Extend it to zero one score interval before the first centre and after the last; these closing endpoints are not observations.

Construct both representations from the same frequency table. The guided siblings example uses half-integer boundaries, heights 4, 6, 2, 0, 3 and polygon vertices (-1,0), (0,4), (1,6), (2,2), (3,0), (4,3), (5,0).

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The supplied theory, demonstration, guided grid and responses consistently teach constructing frequency histograms and polygons from numerical frequency tables. Students use midpoint boundaries, frequency-height columns, preserved zero-frequency intervals and column-centre polygon vertices with explicit closing endpoints. The guided answers and editable diagram agree with the table. Representation construction is the central taught task; graph conventions support that construction.

teachingContexts.title: Cumulative Frequency Histograms and Ogives

methods.statement: Calculate cumulative frequency by successively adding frequencies in ascending score order. The model frequencies 4, 6, 7, 10 and 5 produce running totals 4, 10, 17, 27 and 32.
Distinguish strict and inclusive thresholds: scores less than 6 use the total through 5, giving 10 students; scores of 6 or fewer include score 6, giving 17 students.
Recover an individual frequency by subtracting the preceding cumulative total: exactly 6 is 17 − 10 = 7 students.

Construct a cumulative frequency histogram with adjoining score intervals and running totals as column heights. The model uses boundaries 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5 and 8.5, with heights 4, 10, 17, 27 and 32.

Construct an ogive by starting at the first lower boundary with cumulative frequency zero, then joining cumulative totals at upper column boundaries. The model joins (3.5, 0), (4.5, 4), (5.5, 10), (6.5, 17), (7.5, 27) and (8.5, 32), finishing at the total.
Use the supplied graph title, labelled score and cumulative-frequency axes, and consistent scales to position histogram boundaries and ogive points.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching links cumulative tables, threshold interpretation and frequency recovery to cumulative histograms and ogives. Guided responses consistently demonstrate running totals, strict versus inclusive counts, subtraction of adjacent totals, and plotting at upper boundaries with an initial zero point. The supplied graph model agrees with the table and worked response.

teachingContexts.title: Choosing an Appropriate Graph

methods.statement: Choose and justify a graph according to the question being answered and the information the display should emphasise.
Use a column graph to compare quantities by heights measured from the same baseline. A pictogram compares symbols and requires a key; a table retains individual values.
Use a line graph to show change over time, joining readings in meaningful time order. Avoid joining unrelated colour categories because connections imply an order and intermediate values.

Use a dot plot, stem-and-leaf plot, histogram or frequency polygon to show a numerical distribution, including shape, spread, clusters and gaps. Stem-and-leaf plots retain exact values; histograms suit larger datasets.
Use a sector graph or divided bar graph to show category proportions of a whole. The guided example selects a sector graph to show Week 1's share of total skateboard sales.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching focuses on choosing and explaining suitable graphs by purpose: comparing quantities, showing change over time, displaying numerical distributions and showing parts of a whole. The skateboard dataset contains weekly sales of 10, 20, 30 and 40, correctly totalling 100. All supplied theory, model data and guided responses are consistent with these methods.

teachingContexts.title: Pictograms

methods.statement: Read the key to determine the frequency represented by each whole symbol.
A half-symbol represents half the key value, and a quarter-symbol represents one quarter.
Construct a pictogram by dividing each frequency by the key value. With one basketball representing 2 goals, Kat requires 3 symbols, Sophie 2 whole symbols and a half, and Ava 4 symbols.
Use equal-size symbols, aligned category rows and a clear key.

teachingContexts.teachingSummary: The teaching covers interpreting a pictogram key, proportional partial symbols, and constructing a pictogram from frequencies using consistent symbols and aligned rows. The guided task, short answer, worked response and completed native diagram agree: 6, 5 and 8 goals correspond to 3, 2.5 and 4 basketballs, with a half basketball representing 1 goal.
