questions.note: Apply the taught quantity/count/measurement versus name/description test. All eight short answers and worked explanations agree with this method. Mass, price, TV-set counts, rainfall, sets won and speed assess numerical classification; computer brands and causes assess categorical classification. The question directly assesses the taught numerical/categorical distinction without requiring variable definitions or subtypes.

Use distinct whole-number counts for homes, people, accidents, students and seats; use possible values across a range for the measured quantities. All ten supplied answers and explanations are consistent with the teaching. The assessed task is discrete/continuous subtype classification. Numerical status is supplied in the shared stem, so numerical/categorical classification is a prerequisite rather than a separately assessed secondary skill.

Check whether the categories themselves have a natural order. Travel methods, suburbs, brands, gender categories and favourite teams are nominal; grades, fan settings, satisfaction levels, medals and drink sizes are ordinal. All ten supplied answers agree. The question directly assesses nominal/ordinal subtypes through unordered names and ordered categories. Categorical status is given in the stem, so the existing numerical/categorical secondary tag is unnecessary.

Travel time generates measured numerical values; favourite colour, car type and dog type generate category labels. Answer C and its worked explanation are consistent with the supplied teaching. Selecting the survey question that generates numerical data assesses classification by the meaning of the anticipated responses. Neither defining a variable nor classifying its subtype is requested.

Apply the taught distinction between names/categories and quantities. Answer D and its explanation are consistent with all four options. The task assesses which survey produces categorical responses. It does not request subtype classification or a definition of a variable.

Use counting versus measurement for numerical subtypes and natural ordering for categorical subtypes. All twenty supplied answers follow these methods; ordering yes/maybe/no by willingness is consistent with the stated context. All parts a–t explicitly assess numerical/categorical classification and the corresponding subtype. Subtype classification is the most advanced assessed skill and therefore primary.

Consider all four categories together. They have no single natural ranking, so the supplied categorical nominal answer is consistent with the teaching. Classifying the poll's data assesses categorical identification and nominal/ordinal discrimination. The taught natural-order test makes subtype classification primary.

The recorded responses are restricted to 5 km, 10 km, 15 km or 20 km, giving separate numerical values. The supplied numerical discrete answer explicitly distinguishes this response set from unrestricted continuous distance and is consistent with the taught definitions. The poll directly assesses numerical identification and discrete/continuous discrimination for constrained responses. Subtype classification is primary; no numerical calculation is assessed.

The supplied answers correctly explain that vehicle identifiers have no inherent ranking. This follows the taught use of category meaning, rather than alphabetical or numerical sorting, to determine ordinal status. The assessed decision is nominal versus ordinal: Freddy already identifies the data as categorical. Numerical/categorical classification is supporting context rather than a separate assessed task.

Categorical ordinal and C. Agree are consistent with the supplied five-position scale and the taught natural-order criterion. Part a assesses categorical classification and the ordinal subtype. Part b reinforces the meaning and order of those categories; reading this response scale does not separately assess interpretation of a statistical graph.

The supplied answers are consistent: unrestricted area measurements are continuous, while the explicitly whole-number recorded values in part b are discrete. The explanation correctly concerns the recorded data. Both parts assess numerical classification and discrete/continuous subtypes. The change in recording restriction makes subtype classification the main and most advanced assessed skill.

The supplied answer correctly orders the frequency categories from never to consistently, following the taught natural-order method. The question assesses categorical data and its ordinal subtype. Classification follows the meanings of the letter codes, with subtype classification the most advanced assessed skill.

The answer correctly uses whole-number counts of brothers to justify numerical discrete classification. The response requires classification of a count at both levels of the taught hierarchy; identifying the discrete subtype is the most advanced assessed skill.

Answer A is consistent with the taught natural-order criterion: hair colours are unordered categories, whereas small, medium and large are ordered. The question explicitly assesses categorical and nominal classification. Nominal versus ordinal discrimination is the most advanced demand; graph skills are not assessed.

Answer A and its explanation correctly distinguish unordered colours from ordered sizes and numerical measurements or counts. Both categorical classification and the nominal subtype are explicitly assessed through recorded values. Subtype classification is primary, consistent with the exercise's two-level hierarchy.

All four answers give the correct requested classification. The additional ordinal descriptions and distinctions between whole-unit records and continuous measured quantities are consistent with the supplied teaching context and do not change the question's assessed demand. The shared stem explicitly requests only categorical or numerical classification: shoe-size labels and homework categories are categorical; centimetres and whole hours are numerical. Subtype details in the supplied answers do not add an assessed subtype task.
